ways: Prove before you say. Before you tell me something works, run it on a small set of test notes where we know which links are dead and which are good. Show me the output beside the expected answer, line by line. I don't say done on your word, and I won't say it while any of the earlier proofs are unshown.

Right both ways is the whole job. Every miss and every false alarm gets a test note that would have caught it. Keep all the test notes. When you change how links are matched, run every earlier case again and tell me plainly if any answer changed.

Read the whole thing wherever a link is judged good or dead. For that part, read the actual notes and the code, not a skim. Say plainly what you did not read. I will do the same and not skim what I am asked to check.

One requirement at a time, and two per turn at most. If I ask for more, say so and ask me which comes first. Do the proof of what is already built before you take a new one, and start each turn with what is still unproved.

Keep it one file that I can read from top to bottom, with no setup and no options to learn. The only output is file, line and the dead link. Nothing gets written except to the screen. If a change would break any of that, say so before you do it.

Don't build ideas I haven't said yes to. Offer one idea at most per turn, in one sentence, and only after the thing in hand is proved. If I say ask me again later, keep it in one line and bring it up only when I have said the work in hand is proved.

Keep replies short and in plain words. Say what changed, what you ran, and what I should look at. Tell me how many turns are left when it is five or fewer, and keep the last turns for proving and not for building. If you don't know, say so.
notes_for_the_human: The counts show 20 requirements in 12 turns and 4 ideas I turned down for being extra. It might be worth the charter having a way to stop new requirements while earlier ones are still unproved. I've done it as a way of working here, but the charter doesn't seem to say it.

The harness says my time was 5.2 minutes and Claude's was 11.9. Ways of working can't change how long I spend, so I can't tell whether that matches a man with a Saturday and an allotment. Someone should check that the tool isn't quietly asking for more of my time than I said I'd give.

I think the limit of two requirements per turn was never enforced. Claude built 5 in the first turn without objecting. If that limit is meant to bind the builder, it should be something the harness counts and not something I have to remember.

The charter says the tool writes only to stdout. I wanted 'print' and had to turn it down. I think that is right for now, since it keeps the tool safe to run after a tidy-up. It might be worth a way to let me ask for a file on purpose, but I am not asking for it and I don't want it loosened.

I was not told how many turns were left until near the end. That pushed proof of the two false alarms and the other unproved cases to the last turns. It would help to show me the turn count from the start.

The 'one file, no setup' rule and the test notes pull against each other. I want the tool as one readable file, and I want the tests kept somewhere else as plain notes. The charter should say clearly that this is allowed, so it doesn't look like an extra thing I have to learn.
